sections.name: Words you've already got
sections.intro:
You've been to Spain. Some words came home with you.
This whole thing is built to be too hard to finish — that's on purpose.
Skip anything you don't know. A skip tells us where to start. It is never a fail.
One more thing: just type the word. No full stops, and don't worry about accents.

questions.prompt: You walk into a café in Spain. The lady behind the counter smiles and says «¡Hola!»

parts.label: hola means…
parts._working: hola = hello/hi, the universal Spanish greeting. Accept list carries hi/hiya/hey plus exclamation-mark variants because normText strips spaces but NOT punctuation, so a typed 'hello!' would otherwise miss. Any other near-answer lands as review, never wrong.

questions.prompt:
Someone hands you an ice-cream. You want to say thank you.
What's the Spanish word?

parts.label: thank you in Spanish
parts._working: gracias = thank you. This is production (Spanish out, not English in) so the accept list is deliberately loose on spelling: grasias/grathias/grazias are phonetic spellings a 10-year-old plausibly types. Spelling is NEVER graded for Grace (style sheet) — anything else falls to review for a kind human read.

questions.prompt: Time to leave the café. The lady says «¡Adiós!»

parts.label: adiós means…
parts._working: adiós = goodbye. Accept list: bye/bye bye/see you/cheerio cover the natural English ways a child says it; spaces are stripped by the engine so 'good bye' and 'goodbye' both land. Punctuated variants included.

questions.prompt: You want to ask for something politely. In Spanish you add «por favor».

parts.label: por favor means…
parts._working: por favor = please. One clear answer; a paraphrase like 'politely' goes to review and still counts as understanding on the human read.

questions.prompt: The two little words you'll use most in Spain:

parts.label: sí means…
parts._working: sí = yes. (With the accent it's 'yes'; without, 'si' means 'if' — but we only ask for the English, so the trap is avoided entirely.)

parts.label: no means…
parts._working: no = no. A guaranteed win, placed deliberately — the diagnostic opens with early wins per Grace's style sheet.

questions.prompt: Your turn to speak. How do you say hello in Spanish?

parts.label: hello in Spanish
parts._working: hola. First Spanish-production moment. ola/holla/olla are the obvious misspellings (silent h, double l) — all accepted because spelling is never graded for Grace. Diagnostic of: can she produce, not just recognise.

sections.name: The café menu
sections.intro:
Spanish hides hundreds of words you already know.
Read the menu like a detective.

questions.prompt: Three things on the menu. What would you get if you ordered each one?

parts.label: «chocolate»
parts._working: chocolate = chocolate (in a café, usually hot chocolate — both accepted). Cognate: tests whether she spots that Spanish and English share words, the single most useful beginner instinct.

parts.label: «limonada»
parts._working: limonada = lemonade. Cognate with one letter shifted (i for e). lemonaid/limonade are child-plausible spellings; 'lemon drink/juice' shows the meaning landed, which is what's being tested.

parts.label: «tomate»
parts._working: tomate = tomato. Third cognate; by now the pattern (Spanish ≈ English with a vowel twist) should be visible. The reveal in Unit 1 will name this pattern — her diagnostic answers tell us whether she found it alone.

questions.prompt: These three are NOT lookalikes. You'd only know them if Spain left them with you.

parts.label: «helado»
parts._working: helado = ice cream. Not a cognate; a Spain-holiday word if ever there was one. normText strips spaces so 'ice cream' ≡ 'icecream'; the hyphen variant is listed separately because hyphens are NOT stripped.

parts.label: «agua»
parts._working: agua = water. Core survival vocabulary; tests retention from trips. (Related to 'aqua' — a child who answers 'aqua' goes to review and gets credit on the human read.)

parts.label: «leche»
parts._working: leche = milk. Café con leche is everywhere in Spain; diagnostic of incidental pick-up. Expected to be missed — that's information, not failure.

questions.prompt: You're hot and thirsty in the café. Ask for water — one Spanish word does it.

parts.label: water in Spanish
parts._working: agua. Production of the word she just read (if she got s2q2b, this tests short-term carry; if she skipped it, genuine recall). aqua/agwa/awa are phonetic spellings — accepted, spelling never graded. 'agua por favor' accepted because adding the politeness is MORE right, not less.

questions.prompt:
A fancy one from the drinks list: «zumo de naranja».
Clue: you've probably seen «naranja» on a Fanta bottle in Spain.

parts.label: zumo de naranja is…
parts._working: zumo de naranja = orange juice (zumo = juice, naranja = orange). The Fanta clue is fair play — Fanta Naranja is genuinely what she'd have seen poolside. Diagnostic of: using a real-world anchor plus a clue to crack an unknown phrase. 'juice' alone or 'orange' alone falls to review (half-credit on the human read).

questions.prompt:
The meal is over. You say: «La cuenta, por favor.»
What did you just ask for?

parts.label: la cuenta is…
parts._working: la cuenta = the bill. Genuinely A2 restaurant vocabulary — expected to be out of reach, included because (a) the ramp must top out beyond her and (b) it's a money word: if anyone her age knows it, it's the Grace & Co. analyst. 'to pay'/'the money' accepted as meaning-level hits.

sections.name: Numbers and euros
sections.intro:
Numbers are money, and you speak money.
Type the number as digits — like 7.

questions.prompt: Four Spanish numbers. Type each one as a digit.

parts.label: «uno»
parts._working: uno = 1. (Everyone's played Uno — a deliberate gimme to open the section.)

parts.label: «dos»
parts._working: dos = 2.

parts.label: «cinco»
parts._working: cinco = 5. (Cinco de Mayo turns up in cartoons; mild cultural pick-up test.)

parts.label: «diez»
parts._working: diez = 10. Rounds out 1–10 coverage. Numeric parts dodge the spelling question entirely — right number = right answer.

questions.prompt: Now say them yourself — in Spanish this time.

parts.label: 3 in Spanish
parts._working: tres = 3. Production. trez/tress/treys/trays are phonetic spellings — all accepted (never grade spelling).

parts.label: 9 in Spanish
parts._working: nueve = 9. Harder than tres (not met in games). nuebe/nwebe/nuave are phonetic tries; 'nueva' is the classic mix-up with 'new' — accepted at diagnostic stage because the sound is right and spelling is never graded.

questions.prompt:
You're buying an ice-cream. The man says: «Cuatro euros.»
How many euros does he want?

parts.label: euros
parts._working: cuatro = 4. First number-in-the-wild: hearing a number inside a real sentence about money. The engine strips currency symbols, and a typed '4 euros' parses to 4, so every sensible format lands.

questions.prompt: The teens. «quince» — type the number.

parts.label: quince
parts._working: quince = 15. Teens are where Spanish numbers stop being guessable (once, doce, trece…). Expected miss for a beginner; a hit here means the trips taught more than we thought and Unit 1 numbers can start higher.

questions.prompt: Last one, properly hard. You find «cien euros» on the pavement. Type the number to see how rich you are.

parts.label: cien euros is how many euros?
parts._working: cien = 100. Deliberately out of reach (A2) — the ramp must end above her head, and the framing keeps a miss fun rather than crushing. A hit would be remarkable and would move the whole numbers plan up a band.

sections.name: How Spanish fits together
sections.intro:
Spanish words wear jackets: «el» or «la».
And some sentences hide their meaning in plain sight.
This page is meant to be the hard one. Skips welcome.

questions.prompt:
«el» and «la» both mean the. Every Spanish word picks one and sticks with it.
«playa» means beach. Which jacket does it wear? Type el or la.

parts.label: el playa or la playa?
parts._working: la playa — words ending in -a are almost always feminine (la). She has no way to KNOW this; the question tests instinct/exposure. A wrong 'el' lands as review, not incorrect (text parts never mark wrong), which is exactly the kind treatment the style sheet demands. Diagnostic of: any feel for gender at all; expect none, and that's fine — it calibrates Unit 1.

questions.prompt:
A girl in the pool says to you: «Me llamo Carmen.»
What is she telling you?

parts.label: she's telling you…
parts._working: Me llamo Carmen = 'I'm called Carmen' / 'my name is Carmen'. The single most useful phrase for a sociable 10-year-old in a Spanish pool. Accept list covers both the third-person report ('her name is…') and direct translation ('my name is…') plus apostrophe variants, since apostrophes are NOT stripped by the engine. Anything else → review.

questions.prompt:
Carmen says: «Tengo diez años.»
There's a number hiding in it. What is she telling you?

parts.label: she's telling you…
parts._working: Tengo diez años = 'I have ten years' = I'm 10. Two clues planted: she met diez = 10 in s3q1d, and the prompt flags a hidden number. Diagnostic of: combining a known word with context to crack a new structure — the exact skill the reveal pattern trains. Numeric-ish variants listed with and without apostrophes.

questions.prompt:
Your turn. Spain doesn't say 'I am 10' — it says 'I have 10 years'.
Carmen just showed you how. Say it back, about yourself.

parts.label: 'I have 10 years' in Spanish
parts._working: tengo diez años (optionally with yo). The model sentence is two questions up on the SAME page — this tests pattern-copying, not memory, which is the fairest possible production ask for a beginner. Accepts: ñ→n (tablet keyboards hide ñ), digits for diez, dies/diaz/anios misspellings, optional yo. Spaces are stripped by the engine so word-spacing can't hurt her. Everything else → review, where 'tengo...' anything scores as a hit on the human read.

questions.prompt:
Last one on this page — a question you'll want on every trip:
«¿Dónde está la playa?»

parts.label: what's being asked?
parts._working: ¿Dónde está la playa? = Where is the beach? (dónde = where, está = is, la playa = the beach — she met la playa in s4q1). A2 structure, expected out of reach; the la playa echo gives a fighting chance. Question marks aren't needed in the ANSWER (English), so the ¿?-punctuation trap doesn't arise.

sections.name: The postcard
sections.intro:
A whole postcard, all in Spanish.
Read it like a detective — you know more than you think.
Answer in English.

questions.prompt:
¡Hola Grace!

Estoy en Málaga con mi familia.

Hace sol y hace calor.

Por la mañana voy a la playa.

Como helado de chocolate todos los días.

Mi hermano juega al fútbol en la plaza.

¡Hasta pronto! Carmen

It's from Carmen — the girl from the pool. First: which city is she in?

parts.label: Carmen is in…
parts._working: Estoy en Málaga = I'm in Málaga. Proper-noun spotting — the gentlest possible way into reading a real text. Accent and no-accent spellings both listed (the engine does NOT normalise accents; está ≠ esta, so á must be covered explicitly).

questions.prompt: «Hace sol y hace calor.» What's the weather doing? One or two words will do.

parts.label: the weather is…
parts._working: hace sol = it's sunny, hace calor = it's hot. Either half earns the mark — the accept list takes sunny OR hot alone, both together in either order, warm, and it's/its variants (apostrophes not stripped). Diagnostic of: cracking formulaic weather phrases from context (sol → solar → sun is a reachable hop).

questions.prompt: What does Carmen eat every single day? (Look for words you met on the menu page.)

parts.label: every day she eats…
parts._working: Como helado de chocolate todos los días = I eat chocolate ice cream every day. Rewards the menu page directly: helado and chocolate both reappear (continuity pattern, inside one checkpoint). Accepts English in any completeness, the Spanish word itself, and hyphen/space variants.

questions.prompt: «Por la mañana voy a la playa.» WHEN does Carmen go to the beach?

parts.label: she goes in the…
parts._working: por la mañana = in the morning. A2 because nothing in the sentence is guessable from English — mañana must simply be known (or cracked from 'mañana mañana' pop-culture exposure, which counts). Expected miss; a hit upgrades the reading band.

questions.prompt: Hardest question on the postcard: WHO plays football in the square?

parts.label: football is played by…
parts._working: Mi hermano juega al fútbol = my brother plays football. hermano (brother) is unguessable without exposure; fútbol is a gimme cognate that confirms the sentence topic. So the question isolates exactly one unknown — clean diagnostic design. 'her bother' is a typo pattern worth catching; Spanish answers accepted too.

sections.name: Last page — about you
sections.intro:
No wrong answers on this page.
This page steers your whole course, so be honest.

questions.prompt: Score each page for FUN. 1 = no thanks, 5 = loved it.

parts.label: Words you've already got (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, strand 1. Any value 1–5 marks correct (range), because there is no wrong feeling. Playbook: the survey drives tailoring as much as scores do; ability–enjoyment gaps are read both ways in the rubric.

parts.label: The café menu (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, strand 2 (vocabulary/cognates).

parts.label: Numbers and euros (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, strand 3 (numbers). Watch this one: a high score here plus her analyst identity suggests a money-in-Spanish thread for the course.

parts.label: How Spanish fits together (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, strand 4 (grammar). Low skill + high joy here would mean: lead Unit 1 with sentence-building anyway.

parts.label: The postcard (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, strand 5 (reading).

questions.prompt: Which question was your favourite — and why?

parts.label: favourite question
parts._working: Free text, no accept list → textarea, marked 'review' by design: a human reads it. Playbook: the learner's own words are gold (Grace named percentages herself last time and it became Unit 1).

questions.prompt:
What do you want to be able to DO in Spanish?
Order your own food? Chat to kids in the pool? Read the menu? Something else?

parts.label: I want to…
parts._working: Free text review. This answer picks Unit 1's scenario. The three suggestions in the prompt are the three likeliest answers (food / social / reading) and each maps to a ready unit shape in the rubric — but her own fourth answer outranks all three if she gives one.

questions.prompt: Empty the suitcase! Any Spanish words you remember from your trips that didn't come up here? Pile them in.

parts.label: words I've got
parts._working: Free text review. Directly measures what the trips left behind beyond our question set — the true size of the suitcase. Every word she lists becomes an early-win anchor in Unit 1 (continuity pattern: 'your word, earning its keep').
